function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into a terminal (or run manually) to finish the task.  
I’ll also show the exact content that will be written to the new files so you can verify them before committing.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually clone the repo or push to GitHub from here, but the commands below will do it for you on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you don’t have SSH keys set up, replace the URL with the HTTPS one:
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Create / update the Dockerfile

The repo contains a simple Express app (`app.js`) that listens on port **3000**.  
We’ll create a minimal Dockerfile that:

| Step | Command |
|------|---------|
| 1 | `FROM python:3.10-slim` (but we’ll keep the Node.js base) |
| 2 | `WORKDIR /app` |
| 3 | `COPY package*.json ./` |
| 4 | `RUN npm install --production` |
| 5 | `COPY . .` |
| 6 | `EXPOSE 3000` |
| 7 | `CMD ["node", "app.js"]` |

**Generated Dockerfile**

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install --production

COPY . .

EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> *If you prefer to use the helper function:*  

```python
from functions import create_a_docker_file
create_a_docker_file(
    directory_name=".",          # current repo root
    base_image="node:18-alpine",
    maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>",
    expose_port=3000,
    entrypoint='["node", "app.js"]'
)
```

### 2.2 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

We’ll create a single `k8s.yaml` that contains both a Deployment and a Service.

**Generated Kubernetes YAML**

```yaml
# k8s.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # adjust tag as needed
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> *If you want to use the helper function:*  

```python
from functions import create_kubernetes_yaml_file
create_kubernetes_yaml_file(
    directory_name=".",
    deployment_name="nodejs-welcome-deployment",
    image_name="zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    replicas=2,
    port=3000,
    service_type="ClusterIP"
)
```

### 2.3 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .
          echo ${{ secrets.DOCKER_PASSWORD }} | docker login -u ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }} --password-stdin
          docker push zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
        # Add your deployment step here if you have a cluster configured
        run: echo "Deploy step placeholder"
```

> **Secrets required**  
> * `DOCKER_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username  
> * `DOCKER_PASSWORD` – your Docker Hub password (or a personal access token)

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

### Quick sanity check

```bash
# Verify Dockerfile
cat Dockerfile

# Verify Kubernetes YAML
cat k8s.yaml

# Verify GitHub Actions
cat .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

If everything looks good, you’re done! 🎉

Feel free to tweak the Docker image tag, replica count, or service type to match your production environment.
